name: Chegodi
shortDesc: Crispy rice flour rings with sesame seeds and cumin. The Andhra snack that vanishes from the plate before you notice.

image.name: /chegodi-1.jpg
image.alt: Chegodi — crispy Andhra rice flour ring snacks, golden brown

desc:
Chegodi has the kind of crunch that makes a sound. Not the soft crunch of baked things, but the sharp snap of rice flour done right in hot oil. It's a ring-shaped murukku — thicker and more substantial than the thin spiral chakli, with a texture that holds up well and doesn't turn soggy.

These are made with rice flour, sesame seeds, cumin, Guntur red chilli and a little butter to make the dough pliable. The rings are shaped by hand and deep-fried in clean oil until they're completely crisp. The sesame seeds toast in the frying and add their own nutty flavour to the finished snack.

In Andhra homes, chegodi shows up during Sankranti and Dasara — it's made in large batches at festival time and shared between families. Outside festival season, it's the snack you make when someone is coming over and you want something more interesting than store-bought chips.

Eat them plain with tea. Eat them as a before-meal snack. They keep well in an airtight container for two to three weeks.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks. Best consumed within 10 days of opening for maximum crispiness.
metaDesc: Homemade Andhra chegodi — crispy rice flour rings with sesame seeds, cumin and Guntur chilli. The snack that shows up at every Andhra Sankranti table. Ships pan-India.

name: Jantikalu
shortDesc: Spiral rice flour murukku with roasted gram and Guntur chilli. Crispy, savoury and very good with evening tea.

image.name: /jantikalu-1.jpg
image.alt: Jantikalu — coiled Andhra murukku snack, crispy and golden

desc:
Jantikalu is the Telugu word for what the rest of India calls chakli or murukku. The shape is the same — a spiral pressed through a mould — but the Andhra version has its own character. The addition of roasted gram flour gives the dough a slightly nutty flavour and makes the finished snack lighter than pure rice flour versions.

These are made with rice flour, roasted gram flour, Guntur red chilli, sesame seeds, cumin and a little butter. The dough is shaped through a star-shaped press into spirals and deep-fried to a uniform golden crunch. Done right, they snap cleanly. Underdone jantikalu are soft in the middle; overdone ones are bitter.

The classic pairing is hot tea or filter coffee. You break off pieces and eat them between sips. Some people eat jantikalu with sambar as a dunking snack, which sounds unusual but works because the murukku absorbs just enough sambar without fully dissolving.

Made in small batches the traditional way — no preservatives, no baked version. The crunch is the point, and only frying gives that.
storage: Store in an airtight container. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks at room temperature. Do not refrigerate — this softens the snack.
metaDesc: Crispy Andhra jantikalu — spiral murukku made from rice flour and roasted gram with Guntur chilli and sesame. The traditional tea-time snack. Ships pan-India.

name: Challa Mirchi
shortDesc: Green chillies marinated in buttermilk and sun-dried. Fry them quickly and eat alongside rice, dal or curd rice.

image.name: /challa-mirchi-1.jpg
image.alt: Challa Mirchi — golden fried buttermilk-marinated dried Andhra chillies on white plate

desc:
Challa mirchi is one of those preparations that seems unnecessary until you've eaten it. Thick green chillies, soaked in buttermilk and salt for a day or two, then sun-dried until they shrink and wrinkle. You fry them in a little oil until they puff up and crisp, and what you get is tangy, salty, crispy, fiery — all at once.

The buttermilk marinade does two things: it takes some of the raw heat out of the chilli and adds a mild lactic sourness that you can taste in the finished product. The salt goes all the way through. When you fry them, the moisture that remained inside releases quickly in the hot oil, and the chilli becomes almost hollow and very crunchy.

Eat these as a side with rice and dal — the way you'd eat a pickle, but crunchier. Curd rice with a fried challa mirchi on the side is a classic combination. Also good as an accompaniment to upma or khichdi.

To fry: a little oil in a pan, medium heat, drop in the chillies and cover immediately because they splatter. Sixty to ninety seconds, turn once. They're done when they've puffed and turned slightly darker. Eat immediately while hot and crisp.
storage: Store in an airtight container. Shelf life: 1–2 weeks at room temperature. Best eaten fresh from frying.
metaDesc: Andhra challa mirchi — thick green chillies marinated in buttermilk and sun-dried, then deep-fried to a crisp. Tangy, salty and fiery. Ships pan-India.

name: Dahi Mirchi
shortDesc: Chillies marinated in fresh curd and sun-dried. Slightly tangier and more sour than challa mirchi — fry and eat alongside rice.

image.name: /dahi-mirchi-1.jpg
image.alt: Dahi Mirchi — yogurt-marinated sun-dried Andhra chillies, wrinkled and tan-colored

desc:
Dahi mirchi and challa mirchi are cousins — both use marinated sun-dried chillies, both are fried before eating. The difference is the marinade. Where challa mirchi uses buttermilk, dahi mirchi uses full curd (dahi/perugu). Curd has more body and more lactic acid than buttermilk, which means the dried chillies end up slightly more sour and with a slightly denser texture.

The preparation is the same: thick green chillies soaked in fresh curd and salt, then sun-dried over several days until they're properly dehydrated. The result looks like small, wrinkled, slightly yellowed chillies. Don't be put off by how they look — what happens when you fry them is very different.

Fry in hot oil for sixty to ninety seconds. The chillies puff up quickly and turn crisp. The curd coating caramelises slightly in the oil and adds a depth you don't get with buttermilk alone. Eat immediately.

Serve alongside rice and dal, curd rice, or any simple Andhra meal. The tang from the curd marinade pairs particularly well with ghee-coated rice or the coolness of curd rice.
storage: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Shelf life: 1 month (dried form, before frying). Fry before serving.
metaDesc: Andhra dahi mirchi — thick chillies marinated in fresh yogurt and sun-dried. Tangy and sour before frying, crispy and complex after. Ships pan-India.

name: Gumadkai Vadiyalu
shortDesc: Sun-dried pumpkin papads with spices. Fry them and eat alongside rice meals — light, crispy and very satisfying.

image.name: /vadiyalu-1.jpg
image.alt: Gumadkai Vadiyalu — sun-dried Andhra pumpkin papad rounds, pale tan color

desc:
Vadiyalu are a summer tradition in Andhra homes. When the heat of April and May arrives, families make batches of sun-dried papads from rice, moong dal, raw banana or pumpkin — spread thin, dried on cotton cloths on rooftops, stored in airtight containers and eaten through the rest of the year. Gumadkai (pumpkin) vadiyalu are among the most common.

These are made from raw pumpkin grated and mixed with rice flour, Guntur red chilli, cumin, hing and salt. Shaped into small rounds and sun-dried over several days in summer heat. Properly dried vadiyalu are firm and brittle.

To prepare: deep-fry in hot oil for about thirty seconds — they puff up almost immediately and turn very crisp. Or roast on a hot griddle with a few drops of oil. They double in size when fried. Eat immediately as a side with rice, sambar or rasam. They also work as a snack on their own, plain or with a small bowl of yogurt for dipping.

Vadiyalu are light in the way fried things made from vegetables are — not greasy, not heavy. They're the kind of side that makes a simple dal rice meal feel more complete without adding much work.
storage: Store in an airtight container or ziplock bag. Shelf life: 6 months (dried, before frying). Fry in hot oil until puffed and golden — takes 30 seconds per side.
metaDesc: Andhra gumadkai vadiyalu — raw pumpkin papads sun-dried with spices. Fry or roast for a light, crispy side. A summer tradition from East Godavari. Ships pan-India.

name: Andhra Boondi Mixture
shortDesc: Crispy gram flour boondi with peanuts, fried curry leaves and Guntur chilli. The snack bowl for tea time.

image.name: /boondi-mixture-1.jpg
image.alt: Andhra Boondi Mixture — crispy golden boondi drops mixed with peanuts and curry leaves

desc:
Boondi mixture is the most democratic snack — everyone eats it, at every age, in almost every part of India. The Andhra version is spicier than most, uses Guntur red chilli over regular chilli powder, and includes fried curry leaves which add a fragrance you don't find in commercial versions.

The boondi is made from gram flour batter passed through a perforated ladle into hot oil, which forms the small spherical drops. Fried until crisp, drained, and then mixed with roasted peanuts, fried curry leaves, Guntur red chilli powder, salt and a little turmeric. The peanuts add protein and body. The curry leaves are essential — they turn crispy in oil and bring a fragrance to the whole mix.

Eat this with tea or coffee in the evening. Keep a bowl out when guests arrive. Take it in a container for travel — it doesn't crumble, it doesn't go soggy if properly stored, and it's satisfying without being heavy.

The Guntur chilli heat makes this noticeably spicier than most commercial boondi mixture. That's deliberate.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks. Stays crispiest in the first week.
metaDesc: Andhra-style boondi mixture — crispy gram flour drops mixed with roasted peanuts, curry leaves and Guntur chilli. Ready to eat. Ships pan-India.

name: Cornflakes Mixture
shortDesc: Crunchy cornflakes with peanuts, cashew bits, raisins and Guntur chilli. Light, quick and good at any time of day.

image.name: /cornflakes-mixture-1.jpg
image.alt: Andhra Cornflakes Mixture — golden spiced cornflakes with peanuts and dry fruits

desc:
Cornflakes mixture became part of Indian snack culture through the South — specifically through the mixture tradition that's strong in Karnataka and Andhra. It takes the humble breakfast cornflake and turns it into something with heat, salt, crunch and a little sweetness from the raisins.

This version mixes cornflakes with roasted peanuts, cashew pieces, raisins, fried curry leaves, Guntur red chilli powder, salt, a little sugar and a touch of turmeric. The sweetness from the raisins and the mild sweetness of the cornflake itself balances the Guntur chilli heat well — this is probably the most balanced of the mixtures in terms of sweet-salty-spicy.

It's lighter than boondi mixture because cornflakes are not made from gram flour. The texture is different too — more delicate, more airy. Good for people who want something light in the evening without the heaviness of deep-fried snacks.

Take it in a snack box to work. Give it to kids who ask for something to munch. Keep a bag in the car for the road.
storage: Store in an airtight container. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks. Best eaten within 1 week of opening.
metaDesc: Andhra cornflakes mixture — crispy cornflakes with roasted peanuts, cashew bits, raisins and Guntur chilli spice. Light and crunchy. Ready to eat. Ships pan-India.

name: Andhra Roasted Kaju
shortDesc: Premium cashews roasted with Guntur chilli and rock salt. The kind you can't stop eating.

image.name: /images/snacks/kaju-roasted-hero.jpg
image.alt: Andhra Roasted Kaju — premium roasted cashews with kaju chikki on clean beige background

desc:
Plain roasted cashews are good. Cashews roasted with Guntur chilli and rock salt are a different experience. The heat from the chilli gets into the cashew as it roasts — not just a coating on the surface but actually into the nut — and the rock salt adds a clean mineral quality that table salt doesn't give.

These are made with whole cashews, roasted in small batches at controlled temperature. The Guntur chilli is added during roasting so it cooks into the nut. Rock salt and a little lime finish them off. No artificial flavouring, no MSG, no coating of starch or egg white.

The result is a spicy cashew that stays crunchy and doesn't have the sticky, powder-coated texture of most commercial spiced nuts. The chilli heat is real — not the mild kind — so if you're eating these for the first time, pace yourself.

Eat them as a snack on their own. Mix a handful into boondi mixture for extra richness. They go very well with a cold drink in the evening, which may be the most honest thing one can say about a food product.
storage: Store in an airtight container away from moisture. Shelf life: 1 month at room temperature, 2 months refrigerated.
metaDesc: Premium cashews roasted and spiced with Guntur red chilli, rock salt and a little lime. Crunchy, bold and genuinely better than plain cashews. Ships pan-India.

name: Gathiya Sticks
shortDesc: Crispy gram flour sticks with ajwain and black pepper. Light, addictive and perfect with a cup of chai.

image.name: /images/snacks/gathiya-sticks-hero.jpg
image.alt: Gathiya Sticks — crispy golden gram flour sticks in a bowl

image.name: /images/snacks/gathiya-sticks-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Gathiya Sticks ingredients — gram flour, ajwain, black pepper, oil

image.name: /images/snacks/gathiya-sticks-serving.jpg
image.alt: Gathiya Sticks served in ceramic bowl with masala chai

image.name: /images/snacks/gathiya-sticks-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Gathiya Sticks — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Gathiya is one of those snacks that holds its own against any competition. Thin gram flour sticks pressed through a sev press with ajwain seeds and black pepper, fried until crisp and light. They don't feel heavy, don't leave oil on your hands, and they have a quiet flavour that makes you keep reaching back into the container.

These are made with gram flour, ajwain (carom seeds), black pepper, a little oil and salt. The ajwain gives a subtle fragrance and aids digestion. The black pepper gives a mild heat that builds. They're fried in clean oil at the right temperature so the interior is fully cooked and the exterior stays crunchy without being dark.

Gathiya are the classic tea-time snack across western India. Break them into pieces, eat them whole, or use them as a base for a quick chaat with yogurt and chutneys. They're also good crushed over khichdi or dal for texture.

Store in an airtight container. They keep their crunch well at room temperature for two to three weeks.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks. Do not refrigerate.
metaDesc: Crispy gathiya sticks made with gram flour, ajwain and black pepper. The classic tea-time namkeen — light, crunchy and genuinely satisfying. Ships pan-India.

name: Bhavnagari Gathiya
shortDesc: Thick, soft gathiya from Bhavnagar with black pepper and green chilli. Softer than regular gathiya — a regional speciality worth knowing.

image.name: /images/snacks/bhavnagari-gathiya-hero.jpg
image.alt: Bhavnagari Gathiya — thick golden gram flour snack with black pepper

image.name: /images/snacks/bhavnagari-gathiya-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Bhavnagari Gathiya ingredients — gram flour, green chilli, ajwain, black pepper

image.name: /images/snacks/bhavnagari-gathiya-serving.jpg
image.alt: Bhavnagari Gathiya in ceramic bowl with chai and green chutney

image.name: /images/snacks/bhavnagari-gathiya-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Bhavnagari Gathiya — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Bhavnagari gathiya is different from the thin sev-style gathiya most people know. It's thicker, slightly softer in the centre, and made with green chilli and more black pepper. The Bhavnagar region of Gujarat is where this style originated, and the distinguishing feature is the texture — firm and crunchy outside but with a little give inside, unlike the uniformly brittle regular gathiya.

Made with gram flour, black peppercorns, fresh green chilli, ajwain and a touch of oil. The green chilli and pepper together give a real heat — this is a spicier snack than regular gathiya and that's intentional. The slight softness inside makes eating one piece feel more substantial.

Eat with green chutney. Eat with chai. Use as a dunking snack with masala buttermilk. This is the kind of regional variation that doesn't get enough attention outside its home state.

Keep in an airtight container at room temperature. Best within two weeks.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 2 weeks. Best consumed within 10 days for peak texture.
metaDesc: Bhavnagari gathiya — thick gram flour snack from Bhavnagar with black pepper and green chilli. Soft inside, crunchy outside. A Gujarati speciality. Ships pan-India.

name: Fafda
shortDesc: Crispy gram flour strips with ajwain and turmeric. The snack that pairs best with raw papaya chutney on a Sunday morning.

image.name: /images/snacks/fafda-hero.jpg
image.alt: Fafda — crispy golden gram flour strips on white background

image.name: /images/snacks/fafda-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Fafda ingredients — gram flour, ajwain, turmeric, black pepper, oil

image.name: /images/snacks/fafda-serving.jpg
image.alt: Fafda served with green chutney and chai

image.name: /images/snacks/fafda-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Fafda — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Fafda is the weekend breakfast of Gujarat. Sunday morning means fafda-jalebi — the savoury fafda alongside the sweet spiral jalebi. But fafda stands on its own without the jalebi too. It's a long flat strip of gram flour dough, pressed thin and fried until it blisters and crisps.

The dough is made with gram flour (besan), ajwain seeds, turmeric, baking soda and a little oil. The baking soda creates the slight puffiness and blister texture on the surface. The ajwain gives that distinctive faint fragrance. Fafda has a much lighter texture than sev or gathiya — thinner, more delicate, and with a surface texture that's almost hollow.

Serve with raw papaya chutney (the traditional pairing) or green chutney. It also works as a side snack during meals, broken into pieces alongside dal and rice. The crunch is excellent and the gram flour flavour is clean.

Fafda doesn't keep as long as harder snacks — best within 10 days of the batch date.
storage: Store in an airtight container. Shelf life: 2 weeks at room temperature. Best consumed within 10 days for maximum crispiness.
metaDesc: Crispy fafda — long gram flour strips fried with ajwain and turmeric. The iconic Gujarati breakfast snack. Best with raw papaya chutney. Ships pan-India.

name: Farsan Mix
shortDesc: Crispy Gujarati mixed snack with sev, peanuts, fried lentils and curry leaves. More complex than regular mixture — every handful is different.

image.name: /images/snacks/farsan-mix-hero.jpg
image.alt: Farsan Mix — colorful Gujarati mixed snack with sev, peanuts and fried lentils

image.name: /images/snacks/farsan-mix-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Farsan Mix ingredients — gram flour sev, peanuts, curry leaves, red chillies, lentils

image.name: /images/snacks/farsan-mix-serving.jpg
image.alt: Farsan Mix in ceramic bowl with masala chai

image.name: /images/snacks/farsan-mix-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Farsan Mix — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Farsan is the Gujarati word for savoury snacks, and farsan mix is the combination of several different fried elements in one bag. Unlike regular boondi mixture which is mostly boondi, farsan mix is more varied — thin sev, thick sev, fried peanuts, fried lentils, green peas, curry leaves and spices all mix together.

Every handful is different because the components are different sizes and textures. The thin sev provides a crunchy, fine backdrop. The peanuts add richness. The fried lentils add a different kind of starch crunch. Curry leaves add fragrance. Together, it's a more interesting eating experience than a uniform mixture.

The spicing is moderate — not as fiery as Andhra mixtures, more balanced between spice, salt and a slight sweetness. This is a snack meant for long snacking sessions, not just a quick handful. Good for travel, good for work, good for film watching.

Keep in an airtight container. It stays fresh and crisp at room temperature for two to three weeks.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 2–3 weeks. Best consumed within 2 weeks of opening.
metaDesc: Gujarati farsan mix — a combination of thin sev, peanuts, fried lentils, curry leaves and spices. More complex than regular mixture. Ships pan-India.

name: Khakhra
shortDesc: Thin, crispy whole wheat rounds roasted with cumin and ajwain. The snack that looks like a papad but has its own character.

image.name: /images/snacks/khakhra-hero.jpg
image.alt: Khakhra — stack of round golden-brown crispy wheat snacks with cumin

image.name: /images/snacks/khakhra-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Khakhra ingredients — whole wheat flour, cumin, ajwain, oil, black pepper

image.name: /images/snacks/khakhra-serving.jpg
image.alt: Khakhra on ceramic plate with pickle and masala chai

image.name: /images/snacks/khakhra-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Khakhra — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Khakhra is made from whole wheat dough rolled very thin — thinner than a chapati — and roasted on a tava with constant pressing until it dries out completely and becomes crisp. It's not fried. It's not baked. It's a slow roasting process that removes all moisture and creates a cracker-like texture with a characteristic rough surface from where the dough blistered during roasting.

Made with whole wheat flour, cumin seeds, ajwain, a little oil and salt. Black pepper can be added. The cumin and ajwain flavours are the defining flavours of a plain khakhra. Some varieties include methi, masala, or chilli — but the plain version shows the technique best.

Khakhra is substantially healthier than most fried snacks because it contains no deep-frying oil — the oil content is minimal. It's high in fibre from the whole wheat. It's filling in the way whole grain foods are filling.

Eat with pickle or chutney. Eat plain. Crush it over soup as a topping. Khakhra stores extremely well — months in an airtight container — which makes it an ideal pantry snack.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature. Shelf life: 1–2 months. Extremely good keeping quality due to very low moisture content.
metaDesc: Khakhra — thin whole wheat rounds roasted with cumin and ajwain until crisp. Not fried. High fibre. The Gujarati snack with excellent keeping quality. Ships pan-India.

name: Nylon Sev
shortDesc: Ultra-fine gram flour threads, delicate and crispy. The sev that melts on the tongue — used as a topper on everything from bhel to dal.

image.name: /images/snacks/nylon-sev-hero.jpg
image.alt: Nylon Sev — ultra-fine golden gram flour threads in a bowl

image.name: /images/snacks/nylon-sev-ingredients.jpg
image.alt: Nylon Sev ingredients — gram flour, ajwain, turmeric, oil, salt

image.name: /images/snacks/nylon-sev-serving.jpg
image.alt: Nylon Sev in ceramic bowl with masala chai

image.name: /images/snacks/nylon-sev-benefits.jpg
image.alt: Nylon Sev — crispy, fresh, traditional taste infographic

desc:
Nylon sev gets its name from how thin it is — threads so fine they're compared to nylon fibre. They're pressed through the tiniest holes on a sev press, fried quickly in clean oil, and the result is an incredibly delicate, almost weightless crispy thread that dissolves on the tongue much faster than regular sev.

Made with fine gram flour, ajwain, a little turmeric, oil and salt. No special flavourings. The flavour is clean gram flour with the faint ajwain fragrance.

Nylon sev is primarily a topping ingredient. Sprinkle generously over bhel puri, sev puri, dahi puri, dabeli, or any chaat and it adds crunch without changing the flavour profile much. Use it on poha for a Jain-friendly topping. Sprinkle over dal or khichdi. It's also excellent eaten plain as a light melt-in-the-mouth snack.

Because the threads are so fine, nylon sev is delicate — handle gently, store well, and eat within two weeks for best texture. Once the box is open, the sev absorbs humidity quickly.
storage: Store in an airtight container away from moisture. Shelf life: 2 weeks. Very humidity-sensitive — seal well after every use.
metaDesc: Ultra-fine nylon sev — gram flour threads so thin they dissolve on the tongue. The essential chaat topping, and a light snack on its own. Ships pan-India.
